newsitem.title: UK: German car giant warns Britain over EMU.
newsitem.headline: German car giant warns Britain over EMU.

text.p: The head of German car giant BMW has warned Britain it could pay a high price for staying outside a single European currency.
Bernd Pischetsrieder told the BBC Britain would lose its pre-eminent status as Europe's financial centre with business moving from London to Frankfurt.

In a programme to be broadcast on Sunday, he said British manufacturing was already suffering from the strength of the pound which in itself is caused by the financial markets assuming sterling will stay outside European economic and monetary union.
"Britain can't afford to stay out and pay the price with an overvalued currency," Pischetsrieder said.
The pound has rocketed by about 17 percent, against a basket of major currencies, since last August.
"If Britain should stay out for a long time at the beginning, I think the financial capital of Europe will be Frankfurt not London any more," he added.
The Bank of England has consistently argued that London would retain its position as Europe's top financial centre whether Britain signs up for EMU or not.

"Provided we are prepared, as we will be, to quote, trade and settle in euro...then I am convinced that broader markets in euro instruments will represent an opportunity rather than a threat to the City," Bank Governor Eddie George said recently.
"I can understand the emotion that 'we don't want our currency to be actively traded in their market' but I am bound to say it strikes me as outdated, flying in the face of financial globalisation."

BMW, as owners of the Rover car group, have a vested interest in Britain's future ties with Europe. Pischetsrieder said Rover's fortunes would suffer if Britain remained aloof from the single currency.
He said BMW would take the opportunity to export more cars to Britain while Rover, which already sells more than half its cars outside the UK, would find it harder to export to Europe.

That situation would blight the whole of British manufacturing. "You can't increase local selling prices so Rover is accumulating higher losses and so is everybody else manufacturing in Britain," Pischetsrieder said.

A number of other leading businessman, including Britain's Unilever chief Niall Fitzgerald, British Petroluem Chairman Sir David Simon and Toyota president Hiroshi Okuda, have all warned of the dangers of lost inward investment threatened by standing outside EMU.
All these pressures mean Britain would eventually join a single currency, Pischetsrieder said. "You will join the Euro earlier or later, and you will do it at a competitive exchange rate."
